articles.title: 2026 MLB Playoff Picture, Standings: Wild Card Races Heat Up As September Begins
articles.summary: A weekly look at MLB's standings and how they are informing the postseason picture.
articles.body: With the calendar turning to September and the final month of the MLB regular season underway, a handful of frontrunners are already preparing for October while a crowded field prepares for high-stakes pennant races down the stretch. In the National League, the Milwaukee Brewers, Los Angeles Dodgers, Atlanta Braves, and Chicago Cubs have all nearly wrapped up their places in the postseason. Over in the American League, the Tampa Bay Rays, New York Yankees, and Boston Red Sox remain positioned to make the playoffs. Here is where the major postseason races stand as the regular season dwindles down. JUMP TO: AL: East | Central | West | Wild CardNL: East | Central | West | Wild Card AL East The Rays maintain a 4.5-game division lead over New York as September begins, keeping control of the AL East. The Yankees hold second place and occupy the top AL Wild Card spot. Max Fried continues to work back into the rotation alongside Gerrit Cole. However, New York remains without Aaron Judge (rib fracture) and Cody Bellinger, who is back after dealing with a hamstring strain. The Red Sox sit 7.5 games behind Tampa Bay and 3.0 games behind the Yankees, maintaining momentum to hang onto the second wild-card spot. AL Central The White Sox remain in first place as September starts, holding a 3.0-game lead over Cleveland. Chicago has been bolstered by slugging rookie Munetaka Murakami since his return from the injured list in mid-July. Cleveland sits in second place, 3.0 games behind Chicago, while Minnesota lurks 6.5 games back and Detroit trails by 9.0 games. The battle for the division titleis still up for grabs with less than a month to play. AL West The Astros hold a slim 2.0-game lead in the AL West over the Rangers. Seattle sits 6.0 games off the pace. The AL West remains tightly contested as top contenders push through the final month of the regular season, with Seattle maintaining the fewest runs allowed in the division. This is anybody's division as the final stretch unfolds. AL Wild Card The Yankees and Red Sox hold firm cushions in the top two AL Wild Card spots. Meanwhile, Cleveland, Baltimore, and Texas are packed within a single game of each other, fighting fiercely for the final wild-card spot. Boston's midseason turnaround helped erase much of the early damage to its season, but nothing is locked up yet for any of these clubs as multiple AL contenders stay right on their tail. NL East Atlanta enters September maintaining a 4.0-game division cushion over Philadelphia in the division. Ronald Acuña Jr. continues to lead the lineup on offense and defense since returning in late July. Acuña Jr. has energized Atlanta's lineup at the top of the order since returning, with Atlanta continuing to perform significantly better with him in the lineup in 2026. Philadelphia was just 12-19 at the end of April, but a strong summer push has kept pressure on the division race while nearly locking up a solid wild-card position. NL Central The Brewers have the best record in baseball, despite allowing nine home runs in a loss to the Cubs to close out August. Milwaukee has rotation depth, led by NL Cy Young frontrunner Jacob Misiorowski—who became the second-fastest pitcher in MLB history to reach 200 strikeouts in a season last month. The Cubs sit 7.0 games back while holding a top NL Wild Card spot and pose the only threat to the Brewers division title hopes. Pete Crow-Armstrong has established himself as an MVP candidate after completing a 30-homer, 30-stolen base season while leading the majors in WAR. NL West The Diamondbacks and Padres are both still in the race for wild-card spots, as the Dodgers lead in the NL West has ballooned to 9.5-games ahead of San Diego and 10 games ahead of Arizona. The Dodgers have worked recent trade acquisition Tarik Skubal in the rotation. The Dodgers remain the favorite to win the World Series in October, despite their struggles last month. This is a team positioned for a deep postseason run, though navigating pitch counts and health down the stretch remains key. NL Wild Card The Cubs and Phillies sit comfortably atop the NL wild-card standings with 5.0 games of breathing room before the next closest in the race as September begins. The Padres currently hold the final wild-card spot, with the Diamondbacks right in the mix just 0.5 games back, while Miami, St. Louis, Pittsburgh, and Cincinnati all still have a chance as they are within 6.0 games of the final wild card position.

articles.title: Colin Kaepernick’s unfinished business
articles.summary: Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, Colin Kaepernick is back in the spotligh...
articles.body:
Colin Kaepernick still puts in a workout at 4:30 a.m. most days. His football life may be long over, but his life's work is not.

Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, the former star quarterback is stepping back into the spotlight.

His memoir, " The Perilous Fight, " comes out on Sept. 15. And in interviews with NBC News, his first time speaking in depth about his protest's fallout in years, Kaepernick reveals the story behind how he came to take a knee in 2016, an act that made him both a hero and a pariah, and one of the most divisive figures in the country.

Kaepernick, 38, is now also a father of a 4-year-old girl. That, he says, helped him understand he has unfinished business in his life and cause. Being a dad "increases the responsibility and urgency of the work we're doing," he says. He doesn't want his daughter — or anyone else — to think he stopped fighting or that the fight was not worth it. "I don't want my community to watch me and have the takeaway be that if you fight for Black folks, it's over for you," he writes in his book.

Much has shifted in American politics, culture, sports and policing since 2016. And much work still needs to be done, Kaepernick says, which is why he chose now to recount the decade-long odyssey that began with a quiet protest during the national anthem.

Though the years have provided perspective, Kaepernick says they haven't dulled his displeasure with the NFL. The quarterback who once led the San Francisco 49ers on a Disney movie-esque run to the Super Bowl in 2012 says he hasn't watched an NFL game since he was exiled from the league.

"I'm not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well," Kaepernick says. "I watch college football."

(NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has said on multiple occasions he doesn't believe Kaepernick was blackballed.)

On Sept. 1, 2016, Kaepernick and his San Francisco 49ers teammate Eric Reid kneeled during the national anthem before a preseason game. It was not the first time Kaepernick didn't stand. His protest actually began a month earlier, on Aug. 14, when he sat on the bench during "The Star-Spangled Banner."

The idea had simmered in the months prior to the season when, he writes in his memoir, he was recuperating from surgeries. He might not have taken a knee if he hadn't injured it first.

The rehab gave him more free time than he ever had in his life. And in the midst of news of police violence, Kaepernick immersed himself in literature on Black liberation, reading books such as "The Autobiography of Malcolm X" and "Black Skin, White Masks" by Frantz Fanon.

Kaepernick says he hadn't planned the initial protest in mid-August until he heard the opening of the anthem and felt he couldn't bring himself to stand. No one seemed to notice him sitting at first. It wasn't until after the 49ers' third preseason game that Kaepernick was finally asked why he sat out the anthem.

"I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses Black people and people of color," Kaepernick told NFL Network's Steve Wyche. "To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way. There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder."

Kaepernick was unprepared for the response, he writes in the book. After the game, he called his partner, Nessa, and mentioned the reporter's question.

"Hmm. Well, what did you tell him?" she asked. "On a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the worst, how hard did you go?"

"I don't know. Maybe a 4," Kaepernick replied.

The backlash was immediate. Fans burned his jerseys . Current and former players said he disrespected the flag. Donald Trump, then a presidential candidate, said Kaepernick "should find a country that works better for him."

"This is not a four, man," Kaepernick recalls Nessa telling him when the news blew up.

Even though the story of the protest has been told countless times since 2016, Kaepernick set the record straight on one key detail: who came up with the idea to kneel in the first place.

Before the Sept. 1 game, Kaepernick was approached by Reid, who wanted to support the protest. It was Reid who suggested the idea to kneel, Kaepernick says. Not Army veteran Nate Boyer, as was widely reported at the time and since.

Boyer, a Green Beret and former Seattle Seahawk, had penned an open letter to Kaepernick in the Army Times, writing: "Even though my initial reaction to your protest was one of anger, I'm trying to listen to what you're saying and why you're doing it."

On the day of the game, Boyer met with Kaepernick and Reid and relayed stories about how veterans responded to his open letter. The conversation, Boyer says, then shifted to how the protest could be respectful of the military.

"I think it was Colin specifically that asked it. He said, 'Well, do you think there's a way that we could protest that's not going to offend people in the military?'" Boyer recalls. "And I said, 'No. No matter what, some people will be offended.'"

Boyer then told Kaepernick he believed sitting on the bench "wasn't the most inspiring" and that the protest could be more effective if he was next to his teammates, perhaps bowing his head while standing.

"He said no immediately, and I respect that," Boyer says, and the conversation then logically turned to taking a knee. He doesn't dispute that the two players may have come to that conclusion before meeting him.

"I remember them nodding their heads and looking at each other," Boyer says. "Maybe Eric did suggest that, and that's kind of what that look was."

After the Sept. 1 game, Reid told reporters "[Boyer] agreed with" the idea for them to kneel. Kaepernick says the notion it was Boyer's idea appealed to the media because the backing of a white military veteran made the protest seem more "palatable."

As for why Kaepernick didn't clear up the misconception at the time, he says he and Reid wanted to focus on their message, not get caught "in a personal back-and-forth over whose idea it was."

Though Kaepernick and Reid ultimately switched from sitting to kneeling, the protest continued to stoke controversy. Then-Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg called it "dumb and disrespectful." Even his parents initially said it was "disgraceful."

Along with the backlash, there was also a groundswell of support from the people he was protesting for, as well as athletes from other sports who joined the effort.

"Oftentimes, we hear a lot of the side of the pushback, but I think what's disconnected from a lot of that is actually the response directly in communities that we were seeing, and the momentum and the excitement around the effort of no, we're actually going to change this," Kaepernick told NBC News during a recent sit-down.

Those who condemned his protest chose to focus on his kneeling during the anthem — as opposed to the police violence that drove him to do it.

"The critique of the method is a way to distract from the actual message," Kaepernick says. "The conversation that was being had is taking a knee is more problematic than Black people being killed. Just simply put, 'Hey, we need to talk about taking a knee. This is urgent. We need to resolve this.' But another Black person gets killed, and it's like, 'Oh well, that's kind of normal.'"

In most of the coverage, Kaepernick's assertion rang true. The conversation stuck to the red, white and blue, and not the disproportionate number of Black Americans killed by police that the quarterback tried to bring attention to.

As Kaepernick tried desperately to keep his protest on message, the rest of his life was picked apart, from his romantic partner to his clothing choices. When Kaepernick revealed he didn't vote in the 2016 election, ESPN's Stephen A. Smith called him "irrelevant" and a "flaming hypocrite."

Reaction from players was also mixed. While Reid, Kaepernick and five other players kneeled in Week 1 of the 2016 season, many who said they were sympathetic to Kaepernick's cause disagreed with his decision not to stand for the anthem.

There was a group chat with roughly 100 players from all 32 teams that often grew contentious. In his memoir, Kaepernick writes of a text exchange in September 2016 in which then-Seahawks cornerback Richard Sherman told him he shouldn't tell players how to protest. (Through his podcast producer, Sherman declined to comment.)

The tension in the group chat was palpable, one former player in the chat who spoke on condition of anonymity tells NBC News. Some suggested Kaepernick was only kneeling for personal gain, even though by then it was clear he'd suffer a professional blow. In 2017, he became a free agent after the 49ers told him they would release him. The summer passed, and beyond a meeting with the Seattle Seahawks, no teams scheduled workouts.

"I thoroughly enjoyed meeting with Colin, we just didn't get to the next level," then-Seahawks coach Pete Carroll told NBC News in an email about the meeting. Kaepernick says his meeting with Carroll and general manager John Schneider focused on his political beliefs. (The Seahawks did not respond to a request for comment.)

"Which, in pretty much any environment outside the NFL, would be immediate litigation," Kaepernick says.

The same league that let Michael Vick play again after he went to prison for dogfighting, and allowed Deshaun Watson to sign a contract for $230 million following accusations of sexual misconduct by more than 20 women (Watson has maintained his innocence), was keeping Kaepernick out.

"There's not a definitive moment that I would point to," Kaepernick says about when he realized what was happening.

"Coming on the back of going to a Super Bowl, going to an NFC Championship, setting records, and not a single team would bring me in, even for a workout?" Kaepernick says.

In August 2017, the Miami Dolphins — whose owner Stephen Ross previously launched a nonprofit to fight systemic racism — signed quarterback Jay Cutler after an injury to starter Ryan Tannehill, even though Cutler had already retired . NFL team executives, meanwhile, used the media to try to throw water on the idea that Kaepernick was blackballed.

Some coaches and GMs did reach out, Kaepernick says, and explicitly told him, "Yeah, we want to bring you in, but it's getting shut down above us."

One of those coaches, Kaepernick writes in his book, was John Harbaugh, the then-head coach of the Baltimore Ravens. Kaepernick spoke extensively with Harbaugh during the summer of 2017. Harbaugh's brother Jim was Kaepernick's coach during the 49ers' run to the Super Bowl.

Kaepernick writes that Harbaugh was "pushing" to sign him, but was "shut down from above."

In October 2017, Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL under the terms of the league's and players' collective bargaining agreement, alleging that owners were colluding against signing him due to his protest.

"Everybody believes that he was blackballed," says one former player who was in the league during 2016. "Players knew that this would happen. That was a firm belief around the league."

Goodell pushed back on the notion of organized collusion to keep Kaepernick out of the NFL.

"Those are decisions that each individual owner has to make and their clubs, coaches, GMs," Goodell told NBC in 2020. "And I've talked to a lot of our clubs about it and I've encouraged them. I'd love to see him play again."

In November 2019 — months after the NFL settled Kaepernick's lawsuit — the league tried to arrange a midseason workout for him in front of all 32 teams. The details of this day are now infamous, as Kaepernick ultimately called off the NFL's workout the morning of due to an extensive waiver he refused to sign — a waiver Kaepernick believed would sign away his employment rights and potential future claims — and instead managed to organize a workout of his own.

The dissolution of the workout drew another round of skepticism, with many claiming Kaepernick was pulling a media stunt or was not serious about wanting to play again.

While Kaepernick was out of the league, the NFL went about trying to turn the temperature down on his protest, battling the aftermath of an especially divisive election and a ratings slide some attributed to the player demonstrations.

The league partnered in 2017 with the Players Coalition, a group founded to address systemic racism, and has since committed more than half a billion dollars to various social justice causes. Kaepernick wasn't part of the group. (Reid said in 2017 that Kaepernick was kicked out of communications with the group by co-founder Malcolm Jenkins, which Jenkins denied.)

The NFL did whatever it could to stop the kneeling, the former player says, believing the league wanted to weed out players who kneeled: "What happened was the league and the Players Coalition came to a deal, and then the league did what they were going to do … They wanted their games to go back to normal."

Kaepernick's protest likely cost him tens of millions of dollars, even accounting for whatever he got from the NFL in the settlement.

But as his career was sacked, as television pundits continued to make personal attacks, and as 986 people were killed by police in 2017, Kaepernick stayed largely quiet.

"No individual should be speaking for everyone across the country. I don't think that's a responsible way to approach things," Kaepernick says. "It's also being able to enable other people to step into leadership positions, because that's what movements actually are. It's not one person just driving things."

Months after his workout snafu, events unrelated to Kaepernick raised the volume on his protest once more.

On May 25, 2020, 46-year-old George Floyd was killed by police officer Derek Chauvin in Minnesota.

Video revealed Chauvin kneeled on Floyd's neck for over nine minutes, killing him. Chauvin was convicted on multiple murder charges in 2021.

Nearly four years after Kaepernick kneeled in response to police brutality, worldwide protests emerged in the wake of Floyd's killing. Kaepernick says seeing the protests around the world made him hopeful in the moment, especially as people in some cases risked their own well-being to be heard in the middle of the pandemic.

"There was a significant portion of the population that previously was disconnected from these realities," Kaepernick says. "It was like, oh, actually I have to sit with this now and I have to grapple with this. And am I OK with this? And what is my role within this? Am I complicit?"

Corporations also scrambled to meet the moment, including the NFL. In June 2020, several NFL players coordinated social media posts asking for the league to condemn racism and "admit wrong in silencing our players from peacefully protesting."

The next day, Goodell responded in a video message.

"We, the National Football League, condemn racism and the systematic oppression of Black people," Goodell said in the video, echoing the words players demanded from him. "We, the National Football League, admit we were wrong for not listening to NFL players earlier and encourage all to speak out and peacefully protest. We, the National Football League, believe Black lives matter."

"His response through that video was only because of pressure from players, not because it was altruistic," Kaepernick says.

The idea that the league should have listened to protesting players "is so laughable in my mind, and so disingenuous," Kaepernick says. "We had been trying to address the issue that the NFL created with blackballing me for years. To come out and say we should have listened on the back of that — while I'm still actively trying to play in the NFL — it's so performative."

Starting the season after Goodell's video, the NFL began adding messages such as "Choose Love" and "End Racism" in the end zones of every stadium. It continued donating millions to the Inspire Change fund. In 2021, the league expanded on its Rooney Rule, which requires teams to interview at least two minority candidates for certain jobs.

"'End Racism' in the back of the end zone is a great marketing campaign, but what are the actions behind it?" Kaepernick says. He adds that at the same time the league was putting slogans on the field, it was employing the practice of " race norming ," arguing that Black players began their careers with lower cognitive function in an effort to deny them payments as a result of a 2013 concussion lawsuit. (The NFL halted the practice in 2021.)

"I don't think the NFL has materially changed. None of their actions show that," Kaepernick says. "We have seen it time and time again. For them, it has gone back to business as usual, and I think that is a tragedy that we have allowed them to be able to get to that point."

In a statement to NBC News, the NFL said: "The issues Colin and other NFL players raised remain important to the league and deserving of continued attention and action," noting the league still works with Inspire Change to "support meaningful progress."

The NFL added: "Since 2017, that work has reached thousands of national and grassroots partners, backed by more than $575 million in contributions. We remain committed to listening, collaborating, and taking action that creates lasting impact."

While 2020 appeared to cast Kaepernick's protest in a more favorable light, the country's collective backlash seemed even more pronounced after Trump was elected to a second term.

Many corporations and college campuses rolled back their diversity, equity and inclusion practices. Many politicians disavowed or walked back their anti-police stances from the aftermath of Floyd's death.

Meanwhile, high-profile athletes, including some who supported Kaepernick, have retreated on taking political stances on issues such as the killing of Americans by immigration enforcement agents this year.

"We have seen on the corporate side a shift in capitulation to the administration," Kaepernick says, which he says in turn has had an effect on athletes.

In this environment, Kaepernick says he tries to be strategic about when to speak up.

"I try not to just flood things and be a stream of consciousness of everything because it does lose some of the impact," he says. "I try to be intentional. When is it the right time and place for me to speak up on something?"

Though his prospects of getting back on the field have dimmed, Kaepernick says he still trains as if he's in the NFL.

His daily routine typically begins with his early morning workout. Then, he says, his real work begins: He helps get his 4-year-old daughter ready for school. He devotes time to his various business endeavors, ranging from the Know Your Rights Camp to his AI company, Lumi Story, to his production house, Kaepernick Media.

Being a father has especially added a new sense of urgency, he says.

"You no longer have the luxury of thinking about it from a perspective of, it's just me going through this world," he says. "You think about it from the responsibility of creating an environment and a society that allows someone that is like your child to be able to grow up and thrive."

Kaepernick says his approach to politics has also evolved. He's voted in the last two presidential elections and says he recognizes now that the strategy of not voting wasn't right.

Though still committed to his cause, Kaepernick says he often does his work behind the scenes. His Know Your Rights Camp has helped pay for 150 independent autopsies — such as the one for Nolan Wells this year — and has also paid hundreds of thousands in legal grants and bail relief. In August, Kaepernick pledged another $1 million to community organizations.

Even as the country rubber-bands between the hyperactivism of 2020 and the cultural and political backlash since, Kaepernick — after all he's been through — remains optimistic.

"I'm very hopeful when I think about the moment that we are in," Kaepernick says.

Does that mean he feels his legacy is vindicated?

"Candidly, I don't think about legacy a whole lot," he says. "What I think about is what are the areas that I can do work that I think are going to have an impact and help us move towards that future together. At the end of the day, people will decide what that legacy is, and hopefully that's a positive one."

articles.summary: NHL News: Explore the complexities of Connor Hellebuyck's trade request and its implications for the Winnipeg Jets. Former NHL goalie Martin Biron suggests Hellebuyck may sit out if a trade isn't made, potentially impacting the team's roster and season plans.
articles.body: The Connor Hellebuyck-Winnipeg Jets situation has become serious after the veteran netminder publicly requested a trade. That puts Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff in a tough spot, as he will have to balance Hellebuyck’s desire with the team’s wish to get something of substance back if a deal is there.Former NHL goalie Martin Biron weighed in on the situation, suggesting that Hellebuyck may be willing to take an extreme stance if the trade dispute drags on. His comments have raised questions about whether the standoff could ultimately affect Hellebuyck’s availability for the upcoming NHL season.Could Connor Hellebuyck force Winnipeg Jets into unprecedented NHL territory?Martin Biron says Winnipeg Jets goalie Connor Hellebuyck could be out a long time if his trade situation isn’t sorted out. Such a development would have significant consequences for the goaltender and the franchise.Hellebuyck’s public trade request has the Winnipeg Jets in a complicated spot. When a player makes his trade demand public, the team on the other side of negotiations can get a little more conservative, knowing the organization may have more pressure to make a deal.Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff said the club continues to look for a trade that would protect its competitive interests. Simply trading Hellebuyck without the right return could hurt the roster, especially given his importance in net.So Hellebuyck’s situation isn’t just about one contract or one spot on the roster. It could play into Winnipeg’s bigger plans going into the season.What did Martin Biron predict about Hellebuyck?He thinks Hellebuyck would rather sit out an entire NHL season than compromise his position, Martin Biron said. Biron’s comments imply the situation could turn into something more than a typical trade dispute.The former goalie said Hellebuyck has made enough money in his career that he could afford to lose some if it meant missing games. But the cost of that possibility would be high, both professionally and financially.It also leaves the Winnipeg Jets in a tough spot in net without a trade return for one of their most important players.The biggest risk for the Winnipeg Jets would be losing Hellebuyck for nothing in return. A trade could bring players, prospects or draft picks, while a lengthy absence could leave the organization with a roster hole and diminished negotiating leverage.Hellebuyck would also be giving up ice time and possibly significant earning potential by sitting out. This would be a drastic response, not a normal one, to trade uncertainty.Biron’s projection is not to say Hellebuyck is out for the season for sure. It does, however, show how messy the situation could get if the Winnipeg Jets can’t find a solution.The main question right now is if Winnipeg can make a trade that satisfies the needs of the organization and allows Hellebuyck to move on to another NHL team.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Has Mario Lemieux officially closed his 27-year ownership chapter with the Pittsburgh Penguins in NHL history
articles.summary: NHL News: Mario Lemieux officially sells his remaining shares in the Pittsburgh Penguins, marking the end of his 27-year ownership journey. This transition follows the team's acquisition by the Hoffmann Family of Companies after Lemieux's pivotal role in saving the franchise from bankruptcy in 1999.
articles.body: Mario Lemieux’s 27-year run as owner of the Pittsburgh Penguins is reportedly over, with the Hockey Hall of Famer and his long-time business partner Ron Burkle selling their remaining shares. The development means Lemieux no longer has a formal ownership stake in the franchise he helped rescue from bankruptcy in 1999.The move comes months after the Hoffmann Family of Companies finalised its purchase of the Pittsburgh Penguins from Fenway Sports Group. The new owners had previously said they'd like Lemieux to stay involved, but recent reports suggest the rest of his share has now been sold.Why did Mario Lemieux leave Pittsburgh Penguins ownership?Mario Lemieux has reportedly divested himself of his remaining stake in the Pittsburgh Penguins, severing his formal ties to the NHL franchise he co-owned.In 1999, Lemieux purchased majority control of the Pittsburgh Penguins when the franchise was on the verge of bankruptcy and had to be moved. He took a lot of deferred salary owed to him and turned it into equity, helping to set a path forward for the team to stay in Pittsburgh. His ownership group would include Ron Burkle.Lemieux became a rare figure in professional sports, moving from star player of the Penguins to owner of the same franchise. He was drafted 1st overall by the PittsburghPenguins in the 1984 NHL Entry Draft.What changed after Fenway Sports Group bought Penguins?In 2021, the Penguins were sold to Fenway Sports Group, with Lemieux and Ron Burkle maintaining minority ownership stakes. At the time, Lemieux said he planned to remain active and involved with the organization.That ownership structure changed again when the Penguins were bought out in a controlling interest by the Hoffmann Family of Companies. The transaction was unanimously approved by the NHL’s Board of Governors in June 2026. The deal is worth about $1.75 billion.Lemieux’s exit is significant because his connection to the Penguins was more than just ownership. He was a player who won Stanley Cup championships in 1991 and 1992, and an ownership group that orchestrated three more titles in 2009, 2016 and 2017.He also scored 690 goals and 1,723 points over 915 regular-season NHL games during his playing career. Those numbers have him trailing Sidney Crosby in a few key Pittsburgh Penguins franchise scoring categories.The ownership exit is therefore more than just a business transaction. It ends the formal ownership chapter of one of the most unusual player-to-owner stories in NHL history, but Lemieux’s influence on the Pittsburgh Penguins and the city remains firmly in place.Mario Lemieux has reportedly ended his 27-year relationship as owner of the Pittsburgh Penguins, selling his remaining share along with a long-time business partner. Lemieux became a part owner in 1999, helping to save the franchise from bankruptcy. His departure ends an extraordinary chapter that tied one of the NHL’s greatest players directly to Pittsburgh’s ownership history.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Giants Reveal Odell Beckham Jr. Wearing No. 13 Again
articles.summary: Odell Beckham Jr. will wear No. 13 once again for the New York Giants.
articles.body: New York Giants fans, get the Odell Beckham Jr. jersey out of the closet. Beckham will wear No. 13, which he wore in his first stint with the franchise from 2014-18, for the Giants this season, the team announced on Tuesday afternoon. The 33-year-old wide receiver wore No. 3 over the summer, but he had to pick a different number for the regular season, as second-year linebacker Abdul Carter, whom New York selected with the No. 3 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft out of Penn State, changed his number to No. 3 prior to Beckham signing a one-year deal with the Giants in June. For Beckham to wear No. 13, fourth-year receiver Jalin Hyatt had to give up the number, which he had worn his entire NFL career (2023-25). Beckham was one of just five wide receivers to make New York's initial 53-man roster. Appearing in each of the Giants' three preseason games, Beckham logged seven receptions for 76 yards. While he played just five seasons with the Giants, who drafted the wide receiver with the No. 12 pick in the 2014 NFL Draft out of LSU, the first time around, Beckham is second in franchise history with 5,476 receiving yards and fourth with both 390 receptions and 44 receiving touchdowns over 59 regular-season games. Beckham was a Pro Bowler in each of his first three seasons with the team, averaging 96 receptions for 1,374 yards and 11.7 touchdowns per year from 2014-16. Making the Giants' roster is a double reunion for Beckham, who played for new head coach John Harbaugh on the Baltimore Ravens in 2023. The Giants open the 2026 regular season at home against the Dallas Cowboys on Sept. 13.

articles.title: Richard Ríos al Al-Ittihad: ¿Qué futbolistas regresaron a la élite de Europa tras estar en Arabia Saudí?
articles.standfirst: El espejo de Jhon Durán y otras figuras que llegaron a la liga árabe puede servir de ejemplo al colombiano de lo que es abandonar la élite
articles.summary: El espejo de Jhon Durán y otras figuras que llegaron a la liga árabe puede servir de ejemplo al colombiano de lo que es abandonar la élite
articles.body: El mediocampista colombiano Richard Ríos ha definido oficialmente el rumbo de su carrera profesional para la temporada 2026-2027. Tras concluir su etapa en el SL Benfica de Portugal, el volante de la Selección Colombia jugará a préstamo en el Al-Ittihad de la Liga Profesional de Arabia Saudita. La Liga Profesional Saudí sorprendió al fútbol mundial tras la llegada de Cristiano Ronaldo, desencadenando una ola de fichajes millonarios que sedujo a decenas de futbolistas de élite mundial. Sin embargo, la experiencia en el fútbol de Medio Oriente no ha resultado idónea para todos. Diversos motivos —como problemas de adaptación, exigencias impositivas, el deseo de recuperar visibilidad internacional o la intención de no quedar fuera de la órbita de sus selecciones nacionales— han provocado un flujo de retorno hacia las grandes ligas europeas. João Cancelo (Al-Hilal - FC Barcelona): Tras su paso por el fútbol saudí, el polivalente lateral portugués concretó su regreso al Barcelona en calidad de cedido. Con vistas a mantenerse en ritmo competitivo, Cancelo ha reforzado de nuevo las filas azulgranas a las órdenes de Hansi Flick después de seis meses en los que ha mostrado un gran nivel en la élite a su regreso Jordan Henderson (Al-Ittihad - Ajax / Brentford): El excapitán del Liverpool dejó Arabia tras breves meses argumentando dificultades de adaptación y motivos fiscales. Renunció a parte de su salario para fichar por el Ajax, donde recuperó continuidad antes de desembarcar en el Brentford inglés para continuar activo en el mapa internacional. Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang (Al-Qadisiya - Olympique de Marsella / Deportivo): El experimentado atacante gabonés completó una fructífera etapa goleadora en la Pro League, pero optó por regresar al Olympique de Marsella. En el cuadro provenzal volvió a afianzarse como referente ofensivo tanto en la Ligue 1 como en competiciones europeas con 14 goles y 10 asistencias. Esta temporada ha firmado por el Deportivo de A Coruña con el que ya ha anotado 3 goles y está siendo una de las revelaciones de LaLiga. Aymeric Laporte (Al-Nassr - Athletic Club): El central internacional con España cerró su etapa junto a Cristiano Ronaldo en el Al-Nassr para concretar un emotivo retorno al club que lo formó, el Athletic Club de Bilbao, reforzando la zaga de los 'leones'. Recientemente se ha proclamado campeón del mundo con la selección española, convirtiéndose en uno de los baluartes en la defensa que tan solo recibió un tanto en todo el torneo. Gabri Veiga (Al-Ahli - Porto): Tras dar la sorpresa en 2023 al marcharse muy joven al fútbol árabe procedente del Celta, el talento español apostó por relanzar su carrera europea firmando por el Porto, donde busca consolidarse en la élite del continente. Jhon Durán (Al-Nassr - Fenerbahçe / Zenit ( Benfica): El joven ariete colombiano, traspasado en su momento por una cifra astronómica desde el Aston Villa al Al-Nassr, tomó la vía de la cesión para jugar en la liga turca con el Fenerbahçe. Su regreso estuvo plagado de polémicas en Turquía. Polémicas que no cesaron en su paso por Rusia en el Zenit. Esta temporada ha aterrizado en el benfica, donde busca recuperar el nivel que lo convirtió en uno de los delanteros más prometedores e Europa. N'Golo Kanté (Al-Ittihad - Fenerbahçe): El mediocampista galo encarriló su vuelta al viejo continente rumbo al fútbol turco con la meta de mantenerse en la alta competición previo a la gran cita de selecciones. Sin embargo, perdió su sitio en el equipo galo con Deschamps y ahora tendrá una oportunidad de nuevo con el equipo turco que jugará este año Champions. Luiz Felipe & Seko Fofana: El central Luiz Felipe regresó de Arabia para pasar por Marsella antes de sumarse al Rayo Vallecano, mientras que el marfileño Seko Fofana recaló en el Rennes tras no afianzarse en el Al-Nassr y ahora se encuentra cedido en el Porto. Tras su paso por la Primeira Liga con el equipo encarnado —donde registró minutos tanto en el torneo local como en competiciones europeas—, el colombiano perdió su lugar de indiscutible con el nuevo técnico y ahora asume un reto estratégico en Oriente Medio. Al-Ittihad suma así a un mediocampista con dinámica, despliegue físico y recorrido internacional con la camiseta de la Tricolor. El colombiano llega bajo la condición de cedido sin opción de compra, por lo que se supone un paso breve para regresar más adelante a Europa. Este movimiento le permitirá a Ríos mantener regularidad competitiva de cara a los próximos compromisos internacionales de la Selección Colombia en el calendario de 2026-2027. La pregunta viene por si Ríos podrá afianzarse de nuevo en la élite tras el paso por Arabia.

articles.title: Fantasy Football: Justin Boone's rankings risers and fallers after preseason and NFL-cutdown day
articles.summary: The best fantasy football ranker in the business, Justin Boone, reveals his biggest rankings risers and fallers as we get closer to Week 1.
articles.body:
With the NFL preseason and cutdown day behind us, it's time to reassess the fantasy football landscape as Week 1 approaches. Here's a quick rundown of the biggest risers and fallers in terms of fantasy football value over the last month.

Josh Jacobs being placed on the Commissioner's Exempt List immediately vaults Lloyd into the lead back role in Green Bay. We don't have all the information about Jacobs' situation to feel confident about how this will play out, but several reporters have highlighted the video evidence from the case, which could leak at any time. That makes Jacobs impossible to draft as anything more than a late-round flier, while vaulting Lloyd up into the fringe low-end fantasy RB2 territory.

The 25-year-old has been a bright spot in Packers practices this summer, flashing the explosiveness and playmaking ability that made him a third-round pick in 2024. Though Lloyd's injury history is concerning, it's worth noting that he spent months at the Meyer Institute of Sport in California this offseason, working to improve his durability. His teammate Christian Watson did something similar last season and it resulted in one of the best stretches of his career.

Brooks has also had his potential breakout delayed by injuries, but the 23-year-old is healthy and pushing for a significant role in the Panthers' backfield this season. Veteran Chuba Hubbard already lost his starting job once due to injury and spent the last few weeks sidelined with a hamstring issue. While Hubbard recently returned to practice and is expected to be available for Week 1, his spot atop the depth chart is shaky at best. Brooks might not begin the season as an impact fantasy starter, but he'll offer RB3/flex value with the potential for much more if/when he overtakes Hubbard. That kind of upside is worth targeting at his current ADP at the Round 7-8 turn.

Everyone around the Patriots organization has made one thing clear this summer: this is Stevenson's backfield. TreVeyon Henderson is an explosive playmaker, but he simply hasn't proven to the coaching staff that he can be trusted as a pass protector and consistent between-the-tackles runner. For a team planning a return to the Super Bowl, the Pats can't afford mistakes that could put Drake Maye in danger, so Stevenson remains the lead back.

From a fantasy perspective, we still haven't seen their ADPs reflect this reality. Henderson is still going off the board ahead of Stevenson, despite my rankings showing the opposite for a while. You can still draft either Patriots back given the quality of the offense and the expected boost that should come with the arrival of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. However, if you're looking for the more stable fantasy option, it's Stevenson who was a top-five fantasy RB on a per game basis over the final six weeks last season.

This is the time of year where you need to adjust your priors with new information gleaned over the course of training camp and the preseason. One underrated area where that can help you for fantasy is identifying upside backup RBs who are one-injury away from meaningful production. Rookies like Mike Washington Jr. (Raiders), Emmett Johnson (Chiefs) and Kaelon Black (49ers) have won the No. 2 jobs in their backfields and flashed exciting potential during preseason action.

Other rookies like Jonah Coleman (Broncos) and Demond Claiborne (Vikings) might be third on their depth charts but are sneaky bets to assume sizable workloads if their starter gets hurt. Even deeper, we have Seth McGowan, who appears to be the next man up if Jonathan Taylor misses time. We also have veterans like Malik Davis (Cowboys) or Najee Harris (Giants) who came out of nowhere to position themselves as the main beneficiary if an injury occurs. Remember these names in the later rounds of your drafts.

While most of the first-round rookie receivers encountered challenges over the last month, many of the Day 2 wideouts saw their stock rise. De'Zhaun Stribling (49ers) is leading the way after posting massive preseason stats and making an impact whenever he was on the field. In an offense filled with older skill position players, Stribling is poised to start right away and should be considered in drafts as early as Round 7.

Chris Bell (Dolphins) returned from his ACL tear sooner than expected and looked good in the process while teammate Caleb Douglas also shined in August. It's possible Miami's receiver room won't be quite as bad as it appeared on paper earlier this offseason.

Ja'Kobi Lane (Ravens) is making noise in a Baltimore offense that is desperate for pass-catching playmakers outside of Zay Flowers. Malachi Fields (Giants) appears to be the No. 2 wideout across from Malik Nabers, while Zachariah Branch (Falcons) continues to flash on a depth chart lacking talent behind Drake London. Stribling is the player to target for fantasy, but the rest of these rookies deserve consideration in the late rounds.

Tucker Kraft, George Kittle and even Dalton Kincaid fit the mold of talented tight ends who are being selected much later than they deserve due to their injury situations. Kraft (ACL) was the top scoring fantasy TE over the first eight weeks last year and is on track to return for Week 1. Kittle (Achilles) isn't guaranteed for the 49ers' Week 1 in Australia, but he should be back in the opening couple weeks. When active, Kittle has elite upside, after finishing as a top-three fantasy TE in per game scoring seven of the last eight years.

Meanwhile, Kincaid has had one of the healthiest offseasons of his career and is aiming to replicate the early-season production from 2025, when he was a top-five fantasy TE through the first five weeks. If you don't get an elite tight end in your draft, this is the trio to target.

August brought several injuries to star players, including a pair of key young lead backs. Jeanty suffered an ankle sprain that was bad enough his teammates took a knee and prayed on the practice field, which led fantasy managers into panic mode. Fortunately, the injury wasn't as serious as initially implied and he's already back at practice working off to the side with trainers.

The fact the Raiders only kept three running backs after cutdown day should be another sign they don't believe Jeanty's injury is significant. The bigger concern for him might be the emergence of Mike Washington Jr. in the preseason. The rookie is an explosive big-play threat who has head coach Klint Kubiak speaking more openly about getting both backs work. Jeanty remains a second-round target for me, but there are concerns.

Love is dealing with a high ankle sprain and is reportedly considered 50-50 to suit up in the season opener. The Cardinals having a starting-caliber backup in Tyler Allgeier also makes you think they'll err on the side of caution and ease their star rookie back into the lineup over the first month. High ankle sprains can also limit the effectiveness of a runner when they do return to the lineup, so don't be surprised if Love gets off to a slow start before eventually hitting his stride as the season goes along.

The arrival of Stefon Diggs threw a wrench into the projections for Terry McLaurin and Chig Okonkwo, but that alone didn't destroy their fantasy value for 2026. However, Diggs' presence combined with the injury to star left tackle Laremy Tunsil has me worried. The reports out of Washington make it sound like the offensive line is a serious problem that could send the entire offense to the sewer this year. Given Jayden Daniels' durability concerns — which limited him to just seven games last year — playing behind a porous set of blockers doesn't seem like a path to success.

This doesn't mean there won't be big days for McLaurin and Okonkwo, we just shouldn't expect high-end season-long outcomes for them. Though McLaurin is just one year removed from being the WR14 in fantasy points per game, he settles in now as more of a boom-or-bust WR3. Okonkwo is a fantasy TE2, whom you likely want to pair with another late-round TE if you're waiting at the position.

The early warning signs surrounding Evans on the 49ers are not optimistic. The 33-year-old wideout has been in and out of practices this summer due to a variety of lower-body soft tissue injuries — the kind that have plagued him for a while. Evans has missed 12 games over the last two campaigns and dealt with hamstring issues every year since 2019. The veteran is also coming off arguably his worst statistical season with career lows in several categories, including yards per target, yards after the catch per reception and catch rate.

The opportunity for significant fantasy production still remains in San Francisco's offense — especially with Evans' touchdown potential — it's just hard not to avoid questions about his age and durability. Meanwhile, the target competition could be tougher than originally thought, with Stribling emerging, Kittle expected back in the opening weeks and Deebo Samuel Sr. (re)joining the mix, on top of Christian McCaffrey commanding his usual volume.

Any week Evans is healthy, he'll be startable in fantasy, but the red flags make him a risky fantasy WR3. And it's just a ride I don't want to get on.

Unlike the Day 2 receivers, the wideouts drafted in the first round have dealt with a variety of speed bumps so far. Carnell Tate didn't catch a pass in the preseason and the Titans offense has the look of a unit you just don't want to be invested in for fantasy. We'll give Cam Ward and company some time to get comfortable in the Brian Daboll offense, but Tennessee's line might not give him enough time to move the chains. Tate is now a risky WR3 pick for fantasy.

Jordyn Tyson earned a ton of praise before suffering another hamstring injury that will keep him out until October at the earliest. I'm still drafting Tyson at his falling ADP (ninth round or later) and stashing him in my IR spot.

Makai Lemon missed OTAs and some of training camp with hamstring issues, which will almost certainly slow down his involvement early in the season. That makes Lemon more of an upside stash.

Omar Cooper Jr. didn't stand out and is somewhat trapped behind Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell. He'll also have to eventually contend with tight end Kenyon Sadiq, who's expected back soon. I'm not expecting much from Cooper this year.

The only first round receiver who might have helped himself in the preseason was KC Concepcion, but he's dealing with a very rocky QB situation in Cleveland, making him more of a stash pick as well.

The hope around the Titans offense is dwindling, with very few positives emerging from this group over the summer. If the questions about Pollard's environment aren't enough to second-guess drafting him, perhaps you'll want to look at Tennessee's preseason backfield usage. Tyjae Spears played more snaps with the starters than Pollard and the coaching staff continues to talk this up as a committee. You also have to wonder if, later in the season, when the Titans are out of the playoff picture, will they want to get a look at rookie Nicholas Singleton?

Pollard and Spears aren't under contract in 2027, so letting Singleton get some run down the stretch would make sense. This all boils down to Pollard being a low-ceiling fantasy RB3 in an offense that's hard to get excited about.

articles.title: LOVB owner defends WNBA’s Caitlin Clark handling, sees women’s sports as investment opportunity
articles.summary: LOVB co-founder Chantell Preston explains why she invested in women's volleyball after watching Caitlin Clark transform the WNBA's economics.
articles.body: Chantell Preston thinks the WNBA has done a good job handling Caitlin Clark and the popularity she brought to the league. That is ... a generous interpretation. Preston, a healthcare entrepreneur and author of The Success Lie, is a co-founder and owner of the incoming San Francisco Signal, a League One Volleyball franchise. She also owns a stake in LOVB, the women’s professional volleyball league. "Caitlin Clark’s done some phenomenal things for women’s sports as a whole," Preston told OutKick. "What Caitlin Clark has been able to do and the visibility that she’s brought to the WNBA has been invaluable to not just the WNBA, but all sports." LOVB FRANCHISE OWNER SAYS TRANSGENDER ATHLETES 'SHOULD BE ABLE TO PLAY' IN WOMEN'S VOLLEYBALL Clark brought record ratings, sold-out arenas and a fan base the WNBA had spent nearly three decades trying to find. Preston said the league didn't do everything perfectly, but she believes it handled the moment well. "Nothing’s ever perfect," she said. "And I think they’ve done a good job. I think there’s still some areas of opportunity." In May, the WNBA promoted a Fever game on NBC and Peacock with a social media graphic featuring A’ja Wilson, Angel Reese, Zia Cooke and Fever guard Raven Johnson, who was averaging one point per game at the time. Clark wasn't included. ESPN followed in July with a six-part documentary about the WNBA’s growth. It centered on Wilson, Napheesa Collier and DeWanna Bonner. Clark appeared in game and All-Star footage, but the documentary didn't interview Clark or feature her in any storylines, and barely acknowledged her role in the league’s popularity boom. The filmmakers also didn't answer OutKick’s questions about whether they asked Clark to participate. Preston would rather see attention on the league’s players than the drama surrounding them. "How do we focus on the positive, not the negative?" she said. "Talk about the incredible players that are coming in, the ones coming from college. You’ve got Caitlin Clark, but then you’ve also got three or four other players that have come up in the last few years that are making huge, huge differences." The WNBA doesn't need to pretend every player is Caitlin Clark Preston said the league shouldn't sell only one player. "It doesn’t have to be one individual," Preston said. "It can be multiple individuals, but really focusing on what they’ve done well for their teams and how they can help as a whole. It’s about visibility and storytelling." The WNBA doesn’t need to put Clark on every graphic because she’ll get people to watch either way. But it also can’t act like she isn’t the main reason those people are tuning in. CAITLIN CLARK HELPS WNBA SHATTER ANOTHER TV RATINGS RECORD AS FEVER-DREAM DRAWS MASSIVE AUDIENCE Fever-Sky on Aug. 23 averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock. It was the most-watched WNBA regular-season game since the league’s opening weekend in 1997 and peaked at 3.82 million viewers. Fever-Aces in July averaged 2.64 million viewers, the second-largest WNBA regular-season audience of the season. ION Sports left Clark off an August graphic naming its five MVP candidates and fans were not thrilled. It's not just the league that has seemed eager to ignore Clark's impact. ION’s graphic was another example of the disconnect between how the sport is often marketed and what viewers are actually watching. Some people who came to the WNBA for Clark will stick around for Wilson, Collier, Bueckers or another player, and some will only watch games that involve Clark. Let them. But the league is not helping itself by arguing with the audience it has. Preston sees a business opportunity in volleyball Preston said she spent three years looking at different leagues before putting money into LOVB. "When I’m looking at businesses to invest in, I’m looking at where can I get the best return on my investment?" she said. "For a long time, people say, ‘Oh, well, invest in women. It’s charity.’ No, it’s not." It's refreshing to hear Preston say that women's sports leagues should act like businesses. Some of the biggest complaints about the WNBA come from the idea that it's run like a charity instead of as a for-profit entity. For a long time, that was simply the truth. The WNBA has long operated with NBA backing and has reported losses, but Clark’s arrival changed the economic conversation. The league hasn't adjusted to the audience and money that followed. WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT Preston is betting on volleyball following a similar trajectory. She said youth participation and the Olympic audience helped convince her that the sport presents a new opportunity. "Volleyball is the No. 1 girls’ sport in the U.S.," Preston said. "You look at how many people watch it in the Olympics, there’s a lot of tailwinds and we see growth." LOVB began play in 2025 and has announced expansion franchises in Los Angeles, Miami, Minnesota and the San Francisco Bay Area to start play in 2027. Preston said she also liked that team owners hold a stake in the league. "We own part of the team, and we own part of the league," she said. "So everyone’s aligned. When the league is doing well, everyone’s doing well. When teams are doing well, everyone’s doing well." That doesn't mean she assumes women’s sports will keep growing forever. "We’re not quite sure," she said. "Is this sustainable for all sports, women’s sports, or is it just the WNBA?" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Preston thinks the next few years will depend on brands and media companies. "If the brands and the media come together and realize that there’s a great opportunity to support women’s sport, I think that to me shows sustainability across the board," she said. LOVB has to give people a reason to care about its players, too. "It’s our responsibility and job to make sure that we’re telling the stories of those players so they become household names," Preston said. "That’s the storytelling, that’s the branding."

articles.title: Jedrick Wills Gets Encouraging Bills Update After Back Issue With Bears
articles.summary: The Buffalo Bills have received an encouraging update on new offensive tackle Jedrick Wills after he dealt with a back issue during his time with the Chicago...
articles.body:
The Buffalo Bills have received an encouraging update on new offensive tackle Jedrick Wills after he dealt with a back issue during his time with the Chicago Bears . The Bills recently added Wills to its practice squad after the former first-round pick was released by the Bears during roster cutdowns.

The move gives the Bills another experienced option at tackle. It also provides Wills with an opportunity to revive his career after injuries significantly limited his availability in recent seasons.

Bills general manager Brandon Beane explained that the team liked what it saw from Wills during his time with the Bears. Buffalo also believes the offensive tackle is physically capable of returning to a significant role. NFL insider Alex Brasky shares Brandon Beane's disclosure, which he made during a recent presser, via his X handle.

"No. 1 draft pick, I remember scouting him.. Really good player.. Had some injury issues… Watched his tape at Chicago, said his feet look really good…"

Wills was selected 10th overall by the Cleveland Browns in the 2020 NFL Draft. He went on to make 57 starts across 58 appearances before knee problems derailed his career. After playing a full 2022 season, he appeared in only 13 games over the following two seasons. He did not play during the 2025 season while recovering.

Ahead of the new season, the offensive tackle spent training camp with the Bears before being released on cutdown day. Eventually, Chicago released Wills with an injury settlement during roster cutdowns, making him available to Buffalo. The Bills could use the additional depth at tackle. Ryan Van Demark left Buffalo after the Vikings signed him to a one-year offer sheet that the Bills declined to match.

Elsewhere, rookie Jude Bowry is dealing with a left-foot injury he sustained during Buffalo's preseason game against the Cleveland Browns, which has limited him throughout the preseason. That situation could create an opportunity for Wills.

The former Alabama standout brings considerably more NFL experience than many of Buffalo's other reserve tackle options. If he can remain healthy, he could eventually become a useful depth piece or compete for a larger role.

For Wills, the Bills have chosen to bet on his potential and sign him into the organization despite his not matching the initial hype that trailed his earlier NFL days. He started 57 out of 58 games f or Cleveland before injuries began restricting his availability. His extended absence in 2025 also left questions about whether he could return to his previous level. However, the Bills appear willing to take that chance.

Buffalo's decision to bring Wills into the organization suggests the team believes his physical tools remain intact. Beane's comments about his footwork after watching his Bears tape provide another positive sign. For now, Wills will need to work his way back into football shape while Buffalo carefully manages his workload.

articles.title: Colts’ Offense Gets Much-Needed Boost With Three Key Playmakers Back at Practice
articles.summary: The Indianapolis Colts received a major boost ahead of Week 1 as three important offensive playmakers returned to practice. Wide receivers Josh Downs and Ale...
articles.body:
The Indianapolis Colts received a major boost ahead of Week 1 as three important offensive playmakers returned to practice. Wide receivers Josh Downs and Alec Pierce , alongside tight end Tyler Warren , were all on the field Thursday.

Downs is dealing with a minor calf issue, while Pierce is recovering from a left ankle and heel injury. Warren has been working back from a groin problem. Their return comes at an important time for Indianapolis, with the regular-season opener against the Baltimore Ravens approaching.

Pierce's Return Gives Colts Offense A Lift

Pierce's presence could be particularly valuable after his breakout 2025 campaign. The receiver recorded 47 receptions for 1,003 yards and six touchdowns. He also led the NFL in yards per reception for the second consecutive season, averaging 21.3 yards per catch.

Indianapolis rewarded that production with a four-year, $114 million contract extension in March. However, the Colts were forced to wait several months before seeing their investment back on the practice field. Pierce eventually underwent ankle surgery after a PRP injection failed to resolve the issue. As things stand, his return should now allow the Colts to gradually increase his workload before Week 1. The Athletic's James Boyd shared the injury updates via X.

Following such a lengthy absence, the Colts have carefully managed Pierce's recovery. He initially participated only in individual drills after returning. The ambitious receiver has already identified Week 1 as his target.

However, the Colts will need to determine how quickly he can transition into full-team work. That process will also involve rebuilding his timing with quarterback Daniel Jones and the rest of the franchise's quarterbacks.

Beyond Pierce's return, Downs provides a reliable option for Jones, while Warren's availability could strengthen an offense that expects significant contributions from the tight end. Warren's presence is especially important because Indianapolis selected him with a major role in mind. Getting all three players back simultaneously gives the offense more of the personnel it expects to use during the regular season.

The Colts also have Jonathan Taylor and newly signed Keenan Allen available to form a deeper collection of offensive weapons. Then, there's Jones, who is another key piece of the equation. The quarterback is preparing to return from an Achilles injury suffered last December. That makes the health of his supporting cast even more important as Indianapolis works toward the opener.

The Colts have limited time to get everyone ready without exposing them to unnecessary risk. Pierce, Downs, and Warren will therefore l ikely remain under close observation during the final stages of preparation.

For Pierce, simply getting back onto the practice field represents a significant milestone after months of rehabilitation. For the Colts, having three key playmakers return together could provide exactly the boost their offense needs heading into the regular season. If all three can continue progressing without setbacks, Indianapolis could enter Week 1 with a much more complete offensive unit than it appeared likely to have earlier in the offseason.

articles.title: Former Astros general manager Dana Brown defends Jeff Bagwell, says he's 'a good baseball man'
articles.summary: Jeff Bagwell has become a divisive front office figure for some Astros fans, but Dana Brown, who was let go as general manager last week, stood up for the Ha...
articles.body:
In his second media interview in three days, Dana Brown , who was dismissed as Houston Astros general manager Aug. 24 , stood up for Jeff Bagwell, Jim Crane and Joe Espada .

Speaking with A.J. Pierzynski , Erik Kratz and Scott Braun on Tuesday's episode of "Foul Territory," Brown made it clear he had no hard feelings about the people trying to keep the Astros in first place in the American League West , especially Bagwell, the senior advisor for the franchise, who works closely with Crane, the team's owner, on baseball decisions.

"Jeff Bagwell's a good baseball man," Brown said in the 16-minute interview. "I have no problems with Jeff Bagwell. I love talking with Jeff. We have some great conversations."

Bagwell, a Hall of Famer for the 15 years he manned first base for the Astros , has become a bit of a divisive figure among fans concerned about his influence in front-office decisions. After general manager James Click was let go shortly after the team won the 2022 World Series, Bagwell and Crane orchestrated many of the moves that offseason, including signing first baseman José Abreu and reuniting with reliever Rafael Montero and outfielder Michael Brantley . Neither Abreu or Montero made it to the final season of their three-year contracts and Brantley was able to play just 15 games after signing his deal.

With Brown gone, Crane has taken over baseball operations with Bagwell working with the team's three assistant general managers to take over Brown's duties until the next general manager is in place.

"No one's going to bat 1.000 when you're trying to sign players," Brown said. "I talked to Jeff often. I would get his baseball opinion. He's a good man to have around. I thought we had a good group of guys. I'm out the door, it didn't work out, but I thought Jeff gives really good input. I really feel good about his baseball knowledge and his wisdom. He knows a lot about makeup and what it takes to win. Just a good man to have around. I have all good things to say about Jeff. I enjoyed my time with him and I loved our conversations. Always good baseball conversations."

As he did when he appeared on SiriusXM's MLB Network Radio channel with former big-league general managers Jim Bowden and Jim Duquette on Sunday, Brown praised Crane for giving him a shot at being general manager.

"Jim Crane's a good owner to work for, he's very supportive, he spends money, but he has high standards, so you've got to bring your A game," Brown said. "I felt like we had our A game, but sometimes it's just not enough. But it's a good organization to be in, a great fan base, a good city. It's all good and that's why good things happen here."

Espada, who entered Tuesday with a record of 245-216 (.531) in his nearly three years as Astros manager, is on the final year of his contract, just like Brown was when he was dismissed. While Espada's future is up in the air, Brown says he's "a good manager."

"I think he's (a) ballplayers' manager. I think guys like him and I think guys respond to him and I think he's still growing as a manager," Brown said. "I've got good things to say about Joe. We had a great relationship and he's a winning manager."

Although it seems like Brown is on a media tour since his firing, he says he's done with interviews for a while, saying, "I'm on with you guys and then I'm probably shutting it down for the rest of the time, until maybe something good happens with me and my career."

Two days removed from NFL roster cutdown day, the New England Patriots continue to modify their 53-man team. On Tuesday, the club added two more players.

Interior offensive lineman Ben Brown was re-signed one day after his release , while rookie linebacker Erick Hunter was brought into the fold as well.

Brown, 28, originally arrived in New England in 2024 and has since appeared in 31 games with 14 starts. He signed a two-year, $5 million extension with the team last December, and entered this year's training camp as its top backup along the interior offensive line. However, he suffered an injury in the preseason opener and was later released. A rookie free agent out of Mississippi in 2022, the he 6-foot-5, 313-pounder started his career with the Bengals and later also had stints in Seattle, Arizona and Las Vegas.

Hunter, 23, entered the NFL as a rookie free agent with the Lions earlier this offseason. The 6-foot-2, 225-pounder played college football at Morgan State, where he saw action in 45 games with 39 starts. He finished second in school history with 298 total tackles, and also registered 10.5 sacks, seven forced fumbles, three interceptions and a fumble recovery.

The two signings put the Patriots back at a full 53 players on their active roster .

In addition, the club also signed four new players to its practice squad. Offensive lineman Jake Kubas, defensive tackle Jalen Hunt, and linebackers K.J.
